title: POC Weekly Sync - Dedicated Sizing & Autoscaling
summary: Weekly pilot check-in focusing on Dedicated capacity sizing, autoscaling policy options, and burst handling. Reviewed initial benchmark runs, discussed pre-warm and cold-start strategies, and agreed on next experiments for queueing and KV cache behaviour. Action items captured for sizing spreadsheet, 24h stress run, and security docs follow-up.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-03
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 50 minutes
Attendees: Ava Chen (Redwood AE); Miguel Alvarez (Redwood SE); Priya Raman (FinSight VP Eng); Jamal Carter (FinSight Platform Eng); Lina Gomez (FinSight SRE)

Summary: weekly POC check-in to review initial benchmark numbers, tune autoscaling policy, and plan Dedicated capacity for pilot. Discussed burst handling and cost/latency tradeoffs.

[00:00] Ava Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'll kick off, this is our weekly poc check-in for finSight, focus on dedicated sizing and autoscaling. miguel is on for the technicals.
[00:12] Priya Raman: thanks ava, we got the initial run results from jamal, so want to align on next steps.
[00:20] Miguel Alvarez: great, i'll share screen in a sec, but quick agenda — review the 1h benchmark, discuss pre-warm options, autoscale min/max, burst pools, and then action items. sound good?
[00:30] Jamal Carter: yep that works, i'm hoping to validate our traffic model against your recommended policies.
[00:34] Ava Chen: perfect. miguel, run us through the numbers.
[00:38] Miguel Alvarez: okay, so first caveat — these are from our staging harness; transcription and model names in slides might be off, we used the 13B open variant you trialed. median p95 p50 numbers are approximate because of variable seq lengths.
[00:55] Miguel Alvarez: baseline — with a single dedicated GPU instance (A100-80GB equiv), we saw median latency 120ms per token when KV cache hit rates are high, p95 about 430ms at 512 token contexts. When we add concurrent streams to simulate 40 qps, latency climbs — so the key is sizing for peak concurrency and ensuring batching isn't causing big tail.
[01:20] Priya Raman: okay 430ms p95 at full concurrency — that's fine for our non-interactive flows but our billing UI has some chat flows where sub-200ms is preferred. can we get deterministic tails?
[01:33] Miguel Alvarez: there's two levers — increase min pool to keep more warm workers, or tune batching windows to be smaller for those low-latency routes. both will raise cost. also prefix caching and kv cache warmup help a lot for repeat traffic.
[01:48] Lina Gomez: quick question, how does burst capacity work — we saw a spike last week and want to avoid cold starts.
[01:53] Miguel Alvarez: good question. Redwood Dedicated supports a burst pool — you can configure a reserved warm pool (min capacity) plus a burst buffer. burst can be either pre-warmed (hot) instances or fast-provision cold instances with a short spin-up. recommended pattern for your use-case: set min to cover 95th percentile normal steady-state, and configure a small hot-burst pool to handle sudden 10-20% traffic spikes.
[02:18] Jamal Carter: and spin-up time for cold instances?
[02:21] Miguel Alvarez: cold start on dedicated causes ~30-90s depending on image/cache; warm pre-warmed nodes serve immediately. there's also an option for fast-launch using snapshot images which reduces to ~15-30s.
[02:33] Priya Raman: 15-30s could be acceptable if only for non-critical background jobs, but not for our chat UI.
[02:40] Miguel Alvarez: exactly — so for chat routes set aggressive min and small batch window, for background async tasks you can rely on burst cold start.
[02:48] Ava Chen: cost implications — do you want rough cost delta for increasing min pool vs relying on burst? we can provide estimates.
[02:55] Priya Raman: yes please, want the math so i can argue to procurement.
[02:58] Miguel Alvarez: rough ballpark: raising min pool by one A100 equiv for 24/7 increases base by about 40-60% on the GPU line item for small pilots, whereas burst-only model will give lower baseline but could have higher effective cost for sustained spikes due to provisioning churn. we'll send a spreadsheet with example percentiles.
[03:20] Priya Raman: when you say percentiles, what input do you need from us?
[03:24] Ava Chen: ideally 5/50/95 qps by route and token-length distributions, and any hard latency SLOs. jamal, can you pull the route-level telemetry?
[03:32] Jamal Carter: i have the traces, they're a bit messy but i can extract qps per route for the 24h window we ran.
[03:38] Miguel Alvarez: perfect, that'll let us map to min/max recommendations. also share typical sequence length histograms — small tokens batch differently than long context.
[03:47] Lina Gomez: security note — for Dedicated we need KMS integration and audit logs forwarded to our SIEM, also SSO via SAML. is that supported?
[03:55] Ava Chen: yes, Redwood Private and Dedicated support customer KMS via KMS connectors, SAML SSO, and we can forward audit logs. we'll attach the security packet.
[04:06] Priya Raman: good. on autoscale policies — can you walk through the typical knobs?
[04:10] Miguel Alvarez: sure. the main fields: min_capacity, max_capacity, scale_step (how many GPUs added/removed per event), scale_cooldown (how long to wait between scale actions), and policy trigger (cpu/gpu utilization, queue length, or latency SLO breaches). we also support schedule-based overrides for predictable daily peaks.
[04:29] Miguel Alvarez: guidance: for chat with sub-200ms target, set min to cover baseline 95th qps with small batch windows and set scale_step small (like +1 GPU) with short cooldown (60-120s) to react quickly. for cost-sensitive async workloads, larger scale_step and longer cooldown reduces thrashing.
[04:46] Priya Raman: how do we avoid oscillation during frequent small bursts? we saw that when cloud autoscaler kept adding and removing nodes.
[04:53] Miguel Alvarez: that is classic thrash. mitigate with: 1) increase cooldown, 2) increase scale_step so you add more capacity per action, 3) use smoothing (moving average) on the metric, and 4) set a modest buffer in min_capacity so you don't touch scale too often. we'll provide templates.
[05:10] Jamal Carter: about batching — is there a facility to prefer latency-sensitive routes so they don't get batched into large tokens? we can't afford to slow those UI calls.
[05:17] Miguel Alvarez: yes, Redwood routing supports per-route priorities and separate queues. you can pin a route to a low-latency pool or configured policy that uses micro-batching. that does increase per-token cost so we'll quantify.
[05:28] Priya Raman: excellent.
[05:30] Ava Chen: quick tangent — we saw mention of KV cache earlier, can you unpack impact on cost and warm-up?
[05:36] Miguel Alvarez: KV cache increases throughput when requests share context — cache hit rate is the KPI. warm workers with pre-warmed KV significantly reduce first-token latency. during burst-cold starts the KV is empty so first requests slower. one strategy: maintain warm pool for routes with high reuse, rely on burst for others.
[05:52] Lina Gomez: any guidance on cache priming? we have periodic jobs that prime popular prefixes.
[05:56] Miguel Alvarez: priming is good — you can schedule periodic priming jobs to warm the KV on new or scaled nodes. we also expose APIs to pre-load common keys.
[06:06] Priya Raman: ok so action items — jamal will run the 24h benchmark and share histograms; ava will send sizing spreadsheet; miguel will share autoscale templates and a recommended config for our peak.
[06:19] Jamal Carter: yep i'll run the longer run, will include seq length distribution and per-route qps.
[06:24] Miguel Alvarez: i'll include three templates — conservative, moderate, and aggressive — and rough cost delta based on your pilot usage patterns.
[06:31] Ava Chen: anything else on compliance or procurement?
[06:34] Priya Raman: procurement asked if we can have a monthly reserved commit — we're not there yet, want to see stability first. also need SOC2 docs — can you attach?
[06:42] Ava Chen: yes, we'll attach SOC2, network architecture for Dedicated, and KMS integration docs.
[06:47] Lina Gomez: one last note: our ops team needs the whitelist ranges for subnets — we'll share the egress/inbound constraints.
[06:53] Ava Chen: great, jamal and lina, if you send that network info we'll incorporate into the pilot checklist.
[07:00] Priya Raman: thanks, this was useful.
[07:03] Ava Chen: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and templates, and sync next week to review the 24h run.
[07:10] Miguel Alvarez: thanks all. bye.

End of transcript.
